top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: We assessed the certainty of the body of evidence for each synthesized outcome using an adapted GRADE framework. Certainty was judged separately for OS and PFS/EFS, considering study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, and potential upgrading factors. ROBINS-I-informed domain judgments were used to inform the risk-of-bias domain, while heterogeneity statistics, prediction intervals, endpoint definitions, time-origin variability, and QBA findings informed the remaining domains. Because all included estimates came from non-randomized comparisons in which hepatectomy was usually assigned after treatment initiation, the GRADE assessment was specifically adapted to evaluate the certainty of these comparative prognostic and therapeutic associations.

top_evidence.text: Aggregate timing-bias scenario analysis used the pooled HRs as observed inputs (OS HRobs = 0.33; PFS/EFS HRobs = 0.41). Longer assumed intervals from treatment initiation to surgery and shorter assumed control survival attenuated the pooled estimates toward the null. Across the prespecified grid, the scenario-adjusted estimates remained below 1.0 for both OS and PFS/EFS (Additional file 1: Figure S3 and Table S9). 3.9 Bias profile of the comparative evidence ROBINS-I-informed risk-of-bias assessment showed that the comparative evidence remained vulnerable to residual confounding, participant selection, and surgery timing during follow-up. Although the pooled estimates were below 1.0, individual estimates varied in direction and precision, and the ROBINS-I-informed assessment indicated serious residual confounding and timing concerns (Figure 6; endpoint-level judgments are provided in Additional file 1: Figure S4 and Tables S4-S5). top_evidence.text: For OS (k = 14), the contour-enhanced funnel plot showed asymmetry, with several smaller estimates falling in statistically significant protective contours. SE-based Egger regression (t = - 3.71, p = 0.003) and rank-correlation testing (Kendall's tau = -0.47, p = 0.019) supported funnelplot asymmetry, whereas the sample-size-based Peters-type regression was not significant (t = 0.77, p = 0.456). This pattern suggests possible small-study effects, selective reporting, or true betweenstudy heterogeneity, but it does not prove publication bias. For PFS/EFS (k = 10), the funnel plot and regression diagnostics were treated as descriptive because the synthesis was at the minimum threshold and combined related but non-identical endpoints ( Figure S5 and Table S15).

top_evidence.text: Deterministic tipping-point quantitative bias analysis was performed using the endpoint-specific pooled HRs from the random-effects syntheses as observed inputs, applying the standard maximum bias-factor approach for unmeasured confounding [18]. Full details of the bias-factor calculation and the clinical plausibility grid are provided in Additional file 1 (Methods S3).

top_evidence.text: Regimen-based subgroup meta-analysis was not planned because treatment regimens were heterogeneous and sparsely represented within comparable hepatectomy contrasts. Prespecified descriptive diagnostics included leave-one-out analysis, exclusion of Kaplan-Meier-derived estimates, exclusion of extreme HRs, adjusted or time-dependent estimates only, directly reported HRs only where applicable, and influence diagnostics. Because the OS synthesis included 14 estimates, we assessed small-study effects and reporting-bias risk for OS using a contour-enhanced funnel plot, SE-based Egger regression, sample-size-based Peters-type regression, and rankcorrelation testing. The PFS/EFS synthesis included 10 estimates and combined related but nonidentical endpoints; therefore, its funnel plot and regression diagnostics were treated as descriptive only. These analyses were used to inform GRADE publication-bias judgments rather than to redefine the main synthesis. ARTICLE IN PRESS

top_evidence.document_title: Conversion hepatectomy and survival in initially unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis with quantitative bias analysis
top_evidence.text: The target contrast was the endpoint-specific survival association comparing patients who underwent conversion hepatectomy with those managed without hepatectomy after conversionintent therapy. We interpreted this contrast as a composite prognostic-therapeutic association rather than as the isolated causal effect of hepatectomy. We explicitly conceptualize hepatectomy not solely as a therapeutic intervention, but also as a surrogate marker of favorable tumor biology, successful conversion, and preserved liver function. Eligible estimates were classified according to the relation between follow-up, surgery assignment, and conversion eligibility. Treatment-initiation-anchored estimates began follow-up at conversion therapy initiation and classified exposure by later receipt of hepatectomy. Conditional estimates began follow-up after response, conversion eligibility, radiologic complete response, or another post-treatment landmark. Time-dependent estimates modeled hepatectomy as a time-updating exposure. This classification was used to describe the timing structure of the extracted estimates and to inform risk-of-bias interpretation. Target-trial principles were used conceptually to evaluate whether eligibility, treatment assignment, time zero, follow-up, and outcome definition were aligned [12, 13]. 2.5 ROBINS-I-informed risk-of-bias assessment ARTICLE IN PRESS Risk of bias was summarized using ROBINS-I-informed domains focused on confounding, participant selection, intervention classification, post-treatment timing or immortal-time concerns, endpoint coherence, and overall interpretability. The assessment was adapted to the review question because hepatectomy was generally assigned after conversion-intent therapy rather than at treatment initiation. For each endpoint-specific estimate, we recorded timing and design features relevant to bias interpretation, including clarity of time origin, timing of surgery assignment, immortal-time-bias concern, adjustment for baseline surgical candidacy, adjustment for treatment response, use of landmark analysis, and use of time-dependent Cox modeling. Endpoint-level judgments and support for judgment notes are provided in Additional file.
